title: "Does Vinegar Kill Coronavirus?" - Using Search Log Analysis to Estimate the Extent of COVID-19-Related Misinformation Searching Behaviour in the United States
screen_reason: Search-log analysis of the Microsoft Bing Coronavirus Query Set (1 Jan - 31 Aug 2020). A supervised classifier applied to the whole dataset labels 0.98% (17,288) of queries as misinformation-related. That is a quantitative share of behavioural log volume with a stated denominator, so the paper is eligible; the construct call is discussed in the row notes.

estimates.country: United States (the paper's stated focus; the underlying Bing dataset is worldwide, with US queries accounting for 1,751,769 of 3,830,284 queries, 45.73%)
estimates.platform: Bing web search (Bing Search Data-set for Coronavirus Intent, published by Microsoft)
estimates.measure_type: % of COVID-19-intent search queries classified as misinformation-related (myths or conspiracy theories)
estimates.value_raw: around 1% (0.98%; 17.288) of all queries [European decimal notation: 17,288 queries]
estimates.denominator: Queries in the Bing Search Data-set for Coronavirus Intent, 1 Jan - 31 Aug 2020 (3,830,284 queries worldwide, of which 1,751,769 (45.73%) issued in the United States); the paper says 'all queries' but the count 17,288 corresponds to 0.99% of the US queries, not of the worldwide total
estimates.definition: The query was classified by a logistic-regression classifier as having misinformation intent, i.e. relating to COVID-19 myths or conspiracy theories (e.g. 'does vinegar kill coronavirus', 'hydroxychloroquine coronavirus', 'qanon', 'bill gates coronavirus', 'bat soup').
estimates.misinfo_def: "a first step is to reveal the prevalence of misinformation ideas in the public ... we train a machine learning model to distinguish between regular and misinformation queries and find that only around 1% of queries are related to misinformation myths or conspiracy theories" (operationalised through a list of COVID-19 misinformation themes and keywords drawn from the WHO Mythbusters resource, COVID19MisInfo.org, Islam et al. and Evanega et al.)
estimates.n: 3,830,284 queries in the dataset (1,751,769 US queries)
estimates.source_quote: Applying the final model to the whole data-set revealed only around 1% (0.98%; 17.288) of all queries being classified as misinformation-related searches.
estimates.page_loc: Section 4 Results, p. 5; also the Abstract and Section 5 Discussion and Conclusion
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Theme/keyword list built from the WHO Mythbusters resource, the COVID19MisInfo.org portal, Islam et al. and Evanega et al.; keyword regular expressions used to draw 1,000 candidate positive queries plus 1,000 random negatives; the 2,000 queries manually coded by two researchers with 52 disagreements (Cohen's kappa = 0.946); 80/20 train/test split, tf-idf unigram/bigram features, 10-fold cross-validation, four algorithms compared, logistic regression selected (sensitivity > 90%, ROC-AUC > 96%); model then applied to the whole dataset.
estimates.moderator_quote: The data-set contains queries issued by desktop users with intent related to the coronavirus or COVID-19. In some cases, this intent is explicit in the query itself e.g.,Coronavirus map, in other cases it is implicit, e.g.,toilet paper. The implicit intent is predicted by a method known as random walks on the click graph [10]. Instead of raw query frequencies, the popularity of a query is represented in a normalizedpopularity score ranging from 1 - 100. The version of the data-set we use in our study covers the time period from January 1st to August 31st 2020 and contains 3,830,284 queries coming from all over the world.
estimates.notes: TWO JUDGEMENT CALLS an adjudicator should see. (1) CONSTRUCT. The numerator is misinformation-SEEKING behaviour (the text a user typed), not verified exposure to misinformation content: 'does vinegar kill coronavirus' is a question, not a false claim. The denominator is behavioural log volume - neither items that exist (CONTENT) nor self-report (RECALL) - so I coded EXPOSURE (exposure_type=proportion, i.e. share of COVID-related search activity that is misinformation-related) and set borderline=true; OTHER is the defensible alternative if the review wants demand-side search behaviour kept out of the exposure pool. (2) DENOMINATOR ARITHMETIC. The paper says 0.98% of 'all queries', but 17,288/3,830,284 = 0.45%, whereas 17,288/1,751,769 (the US subset) = 0.99%. Given the title, abstract and the fact that Section 4.1 is a US national-level analysis, the 0.98% almost certainly refers to the US queries; I therefore coded country=United States but reported both denominators. denom_selection=curated because Microsoft pre-filters the dataset by coronavirus intent (partly by click-graph inference for implicit intent), which the authors flag as a representativeness threat, along with Bing's 2.83% search-engine market share.

missed_or_uncertain: NOT EXTRACTED, with reasons: (1) TIME SERIES collapsed to one representative point (the overall 0.98%). The monthly share is reported as highest in January (4.8%) and 'around 1%' thereafter; the authors themselves caution that several top January misinformation queries were misspellings of 'coronavirus' and are false positives, so the January value is not a defensible alternative point estimate. (2) '378 unique misinformation queries' and the top-query frequency (qanon, 4,685 occurrences) are counts without a matching denominator of unique queries for the same partition. (3) Share of unique regular queries (3.1%-6.6%) and of unique misinformation queries (1.3%-5.5%) are month-by-month unique-string shares, a different unit from search volume, and are given only as ranges. (4) Per-state results are log-odds (Wyoming -3.97, Missouri -4.45, Texas -4.45, New York -4.47), not shares. (5) Table 1's country shares (US 45.73%, UK 21.02%, ...) describe the dataset composition, not misinformation. (6) Mean popularity scores (regular 4.85 vs misinformation 2.62) are not shares. (7) The classifier is optimised for sensitivity (recall), which biases the 0.98% UPWARD relative to a precision-balanced classifier, and the authors flag one known false positive ('carona virus') among the top misinformation queries.

rob.design: Secondary analysis of the publicly released Microsoft Bing Coronavirus Query Set (desktop users, coronavirus intent - explicit or inferred by random walks on the click graph), 1 Jan - 31 Aug 2020, 3,830,284 queries worldwide; popularity given as a normalised 1-100 score rather than raw frequency. Ground truth built from published misinformation theme lists; 2,000 queries hand-coded by two researchers (Cohen's kappa = 0.946); logistic regression selected after 10-fold cross-validated comparison of glmnet, random forest, XGBoost and SVM, optimised for sensitivity (>90% sensitivity, >96% ROC-AUC), then applied to the whole dataset. Authors' own caveats: the dataset is pre-selected by Microsoft, Bing's market share is only 2.83%, and some classified misinformation queries are false positives (misspellings).
rob.item6_quote: Thus we created a list of misinformation themes and associated keywords relating to conspiracy theories and myths around COVID-19.
rob.item10_quote: Applying the final model to the whole data-set revealed only around 1% (0.98%; 17.288) of all queries being classified as misinformation-related searches.
